Vignette: Margaret, Age 78

Margaret has been married to the same man for fifty-three years, and she will tell you, without much prompting, that she has always considered herself a steady person. She raised three children, built a small but respected career as a graphic designer, and weathered the ordinary losses that come with a long life. She is not, she insists, someone who falls apart. Which is why what has happened to her since the flooding feels, in her words, "like a betrayal by my own mind."

Two years ago, the river that runs behind the village where Margaret and her husband retired broke its banks after three days of relentless rain. The water came at night. She remembers standing on the bed in the dark, the cold rising past her knees, calling her husband's name and hearing nothing back. He had gone to the garage to move the car and the current had knocked him off his feet. He survived - bruised, hypothermic, frightened - but for the twenty minutes she stood on that bed alone, Margaret was certain she was watching her life end. The house took on nearly a meter of water. Everything on the ground floor was destroyed, including decades of her design work: original prints, sketchbooks, client portfolios she had kept for sentimental reasons. They were displaced for four months.

In the period that followed, Margaret found herself unable to sleep past three in the morning. She would lie in the temporary flat they rented and listen to rain against the windows with a dread that felt physical, like a hand pressing on her chest. When storms came, she would move to the interior hallway and sit on the floor with a torch, which she knew was irrational and did anyway. Her husband tried to be patient, but she could see that her vigilance exhausted him.

She returned to her design work because she needed something to anchor her, but she finds it changed. She works digitally now - the loss of her physical archives left her unwilling to invest in anything that could be destroyed - but sitting at her screen, she frequently loses the thread of what she is doing. A client recently asked her to design a fundraising campaign for a flood relief charity, and she accepted before she understood what the project was. When she opened the brief and saw photographs of submerged homes, she closed the laptop and did not open it again for four days. She told the client she had a family emergency.

Margaret describes a persistent sense that the world is no longer reliable, that the ground - literal and otherwise - cannot be trusted. She monitors weather forecasts compulsively, sometimes checking her phone six or seven times in an evening. She has stopped going to the house they eventually moved back into on evenings when rain is forecast, staying instead with her daughter who lives on higher ground. Her husband goes alone. She feels guilty about this and also cannot stop doing it.

What troubles her most, she says, is the gap between who she was and who she seems to be now. She was someone who solved problems, who made things beautiful, who did not flinch. Now she flinches at the sound of water running in a drain. She startles when her husband comes into a room quietly. She finds herself thinking, mid-conversation, mid-sentence, about the darkness and the cold and the not knowing where he was. These thoughts arrive without invitation and leave when they choose.

She came to therapy, she explains, because her youngest daughter suggested it, and because she is seventy-eight years old and does not want to spend whatever time she has left being afraid of rain. She says this matter-of-factly, with a dry humor that feels like the person she is describing - the steadier, earlier Margaret - briefly surfacing. Then she folds her hands in her lap and waits, with the careful patience of someone who has learned, recently and against her will, that waiting is sometimes all there is to do.
